Hand both to the artifact service's subscribe endpoint; when that service POSTs to the URL, the request body is delivered into this conversation as a <webhook-payload> message and wakes the session if idle. The signing secret inside sealed_secret is encrypted to the artifact service — it cannot be read, used, or leaked from this conversation, and only the artifact service can sign deliveries with it. A watch ends when the session ends, so call watch_url again after resuming to get a fresh one. Use this when asked to be notified when something external changes (for example, a subscribed artifact is republished). To stop, call unwatch_url with the returned trigger_id.

## Claude_Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/fortress-repo

# Working in the Fortress revival repository

The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**brief**
: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.

**original tree**
: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.

**record**
: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).

**walk**
: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.

**compiled path**
: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.

**model program**
: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: the flat program, which the record calls C4 (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a source line of either program.

**one library**
: Interpreter's library, which both paths use after the switch-over (below).

**component**
: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.

**api**
: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.

**area**
: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the run time), the library, or the specification.

**base**
: Commit that your work starts from.

**gate**
: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.

**harness**
: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.

**building**
: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.

**exploring**
: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.

You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.

## How a program runs

Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, run your test on both paths. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

### The phases

Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):

1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
2. Bind each name to its declaration.
3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
4. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
5. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
6. Mark each call of an overloaded name.

Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.

`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. Before the checker, it folds integer literals. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.

Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.

### The compiled run time

`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:

- the component's functions, objects and traits;
- its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches

A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.

- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss" ...`.
- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.

In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).

`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.

### Parallelism and mutable state

Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.

`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A `value` object has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`.

Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:

- Most data is immutable.
- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").

So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.

Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`. The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

## The record

The record's main files:

- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.

Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.

## When to explore

Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:

- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.

When you switch, load `references/exploring.md`. It says which choices are yours and which go to the curator.

## Rules for every task

- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.
- Write the test before the fix for every edit of source code in the original tree. Add the test to the test suite and see it fail through the harness. Then make the fix and see the test pass. An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (`references/tests-writing.md`).
- Assert every value that matters inside the test, with the harness's own checks (`references/tests-writing.md`), and take the suite's pass or fail as the result. Do not compare the output of a whole run of tests with a saved copy, and do not add expected-output files. The gate's comparisons, and a comparison of outputs that your brief asks for, are the exceptions (`references/gate.md`, "Comparing with an earlier run").
- Take the tree that you start from as passing: its suites passed before it landed. Do not run them to check that. Start with your own failing test.
- Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate, a test or a measurement that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it. Run it again only after the code changes. Running a new program is not a repeat.
- Before you investigate a defect, or edit a file of the original tree, look for its rows in the gap ledger, with the queries of `references/records.md`, "Reading the record".
- After your fix, run your own tests. Run a whole suite where `references/tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite", asks for it, and nowhere else.
- Set up each Bash call as `references/build-and-caches.md` says, because every call starts a new shell.
- After an edit, take the step that `references/build-and-caches.md` gives for the kind of file that you edited.
- Run long commands (a build, a suite) in the background with a log under your tree's `tmp/`, and poll the log (`references/session.md`). Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing.
- Before you design a change to the library, study how the library already does the same kind of thing, and follow its way (`references/library.md`).
- Do not claim credit for the revival anywhere in a committed file. If git does not record who wrote something, reconstruct the authorship from the history. Do not guess it.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote. Do not commit scratch: logs, captured output, probe programs. Do not rename a file to get it past `.gitignore`. Each agent's transcript keeps how the work was done (`references/committing.md`).
- End your work with a report. List in it the defects that you found, your decisions, and the points that your brief asks for. Put a question for the curator in it as a decision not taken (`references/records.md`).

## The parts

Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words that you need to understand what the query prints.

The parts, in the order that work meets them:

- Setting up each call, building, the caches, what to rebuild after an edit: `references/build-and-caches.md`
- The Bash tool and its timeout, long commands and polling, waits and the prompt cache, stopping processes, interrupts and stops of the session's process, the automatic permission check: `references/session.md`
- The base and its build, worktrees seeded from it, the old code beside the new: `references/worktrees.md`
- The build failing, JDKs, scalac and ASM traps, generated sources: `references/toolchain.md`
- The interpreter area: walk's code (`interpreter/`), where a fix of walk belongs, its checks at load, its natives, running programs under walk, the microGPT check: `references/interpreter.md`
- The compiled area: the checker, the code generator, the run time, compiled runs, the `fortress` commands, the checker's time after a change: `references/compiler.md`
- The library area (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`): `references/library.md`
- The specification area (`Specification/`), Appendix I, citing it: `references/specification.md`
- How revived Fortress differs from the team's Fortress and from the languages that you know; read it whole, after this file, before work: `references/revival-changes.md`
- Exploring: where to search, what to record and report, which choices are yours: `references/exploring.md`
- Writing a test: `.test` keys, `XXX` expected failures and their promotion, refusals at load, how a defect that you found is recorded: `references/tests-writing.md`
- Running one test, a few, or a whole suite, and when to run a whole suite; what runs outside the gate: `references/tests-running.md`
- The gate: what it runs and writes, the atomic runs, the ladder regression, comparing with an earlier run: `references/gate.md`
- Committing and pushing: `references/committing.md`
- What every report holds and where it goes, findings and points to report; POSITIONS, FACTS and the gap ledger; the queries of the record and when to run each; writing the ledger with `ledger.py`; the repository's history: `references/records.md`
- This cloud platform (the machine, the disk, the network, the platform's stops, the transcript backup, a lost container): the `cloud-container` skill.

A task usually needs several parts, and every task needs `revival-changes.md`, read whole before work, and `records.md`, for its queries and its report. For example, a fix of walk needs `build-and-caches.md`, `session.md`, `worktrees.md`, `interpreter.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `tests-running.md` and `committing.md`. An edit of the library needs the same parts and `library.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$LineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Size")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$ToString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    balanced():String = self

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =

## P-33

- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3: the compiled checker reports no error on the twelve apis and twelve components of the interpreter's library that the distance to the switch-over counts (the distance at zero; F-53 defines it and holds its value). The library's other components are not part of phase 3; F-290 counts their errors. Phase 4, the switch-over: first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.

Meaning: one change, from the finding. The old text said that phase 3's checker "reports no error on the interpreter's whole library". The distance counts only twelve apis and their twelve components (F-53). The new text names them, and a new sentence says that the other components are outside phase 3.

Sources:
- The scope of the zero: F-53 ("its twelve apis and their twelve components").
- The other components: F-290 measures them outside the twelve. The curator agreed that the plan never meant them for phase 3: his "Of course" of 2026-10-26T04:47:50Z, to the coordinator's "the word 'whole' is wrong" (`conversations/02-phase3-exit-foundations.md`, section 4; the coordinator's sort of the findings, item 7). In the same message his goal is "the fuller Fortress library that the interpreter uses"; P-37 holds that goal, so this entry does not repeat it.

- `List` imports `CovariantCollection` and `OneShotFlag`, which the distance checks only as apis, and which the compiled checker refuses as components (F-288). Do these two components belong to phase 3's zero? The coordinator's note of 2026-10-26 counts fourteen components for phase 3. F-53 still counts twelve.
- When must the other components reach zero? The coordinator's view, which you have not confirmed, is that they do not block the switch-over, but block P-12's step, in which walk runs the checker. The entry says nothing on this.

## P-42

- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: `zip`, for one, gives a `ZeroIndexed[\(E,F)\]`. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`. Why: the type group's paper of 2019 (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019) gives every type parameter the default upper bound `Any`, and the Working Draft itself instantiates type parameters with tuple and arrow types. The compiled path departs from the rule: `fortress compile` sets the bound `Object` (`Shell.useCompilerLibraries()`), and so refuses a generic instantiated at a tuple (row 412). The switch-over does not end this departure by itself; only a change of that setting does (F-289 measures the errors under it). Under either bound, the compiled path still fails on `()` (row 339) and on a generic dotted method with one tuple-typed parameter (row 832).

The texts agree on tuples and `()`, and the curator's yes rested on the tuples.
- (b) The old text said "The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure: while it uses the compiler's prelude, it bounds such a parameter by `Object`". That is false. One line of `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` sets the bound (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:372`, `setExtendsObjectPreDesugaring(true)`), and the switch-over does not change it by itself (F-289). The last sentence comes from the same finding: `()` and the tuple-typed dotted method fail under both bounds (F-291).
- (c) The "Why" is new. It gives the two grounds in the team's texts that the finding names: the POPL 2019 paper, "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any" (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019.txt:418-419`), and the Working Draft's sentence "Type parameters are instantiated with types such as trait types, tuple types, and arrow types" (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:68-69` today; the finding cites `:53-54`, before the callout moved the lines). The library's practice is already the entry's third sentence.
- (d) The example "its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`" is out. Since P-156, every index parameter has the explicit bound `Index`, so that example no longer rests on the implicit bound. Element types still do: `zip[\F\](g:ZeroIndexed[\F\]):ZeroIndexed[\(E,F)\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1364`, in `Generator[\E\]`, whose `E` has no bound, `:759`).

Sources of the other sentences: the text at `5da8144e4`.

Question for the curator: none. Each change rests on a line of the team's texts or of the code.

Knock-on, for the coordinator: the specification's callout says the divergence "lasts until the compiled path is switched over to the interpreter's library" (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex`, the `revival-bound` revision). The finding says the `fortress-repo` skill's `compiler.md` makes the same claim. Neither file is a record entry, so this pass does not change them.

## P-58

- P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper.** A native binding is a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, the library's own form, and it keeps that form. This chunk uses them too: P-33, P-42, P-58, P-59, P-84, P-85 and P-155. Only the concepts below are new.

- **native binding**: a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, whose string names the Java code that runs it. Used by P-33, P-58. P-58 defines it; the `fortress-repo` core should name it in one line beside "one library", since phase 4 starts with it.
- **glue class**: a Java class of walk that a native binding names; it takes walk's boxed values. Used by P-58 (and F-32). Define in the `fortress-repo` area part on the interpreter.
- **static helper**: a static Java method in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/`, over plain Java values, that the compiled path calls for a native. Used by P-58. Define in the area part on the code generator.
- **the class loader's stamping**: the compiled path's way of making a generic instance's class at its first use, by renaming the template's type parameters in its bytecode (`InstantiatingClassloader`). Used by P-84 (and F-18). The `fortress-repo` core's "The compiled run time" gives the mechanism; it should use the word "stamping" once, since the record uses it.
- **the array decisions A, B and D**: the open decisions of the compiled path's array design: A, how an `RR64` array made through the generic array traits gets a `double[]` store; B, where unboxed arithmetic happens; D, the sizes in the model's own types. Used by P-84, P-85. P-85 defines them; no skill needs them before the array work.
- **way A4**: the way for decision A in which the class loader stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field. Used by P-84 (and F-18). Defined in `reviews/array-design-ways.md`, section 3; P-84 glosses it, so no skill needs it.
- **the extends-`Object` setting**: the pre-desugaring switch that gives an unbounded type parameter the bound `Object`, on under `fortress compile` (`Shell.useCompilerLibraries()`) and off under walk and the distance stage. Used by P-42 (and F-289). Define in the `fortress-repo` area part on the compiler, where `compiler.md` now says that the switch-over ends it.
- **the overloading check and the export check**: two separate checks of the compiled checker. The overloading check tests that the overloads of one name are valid; the export check compares a component's declarations with its api's. Both skip the top-level symbolic operators today (row 584, row 782). Used by P-155. Define both in the area part on the checker, so that "the check" in a record entry can be told apart.

### Tenet 4. The implicit bound `Any` (P-42). Holds, text. Ruling 4 gives the detail.

- **Default:** stands, grounds restated; "functions" dropped (rq 218; the specification's own callout already says "tuples and `()`"); the flip of `Shell.java:372` lands in 22c. His entry; the flip is a code change the entry already promises.

### Tenet 5. The exclusion rule and the flat number types (P-43). Holds, text.

- **Sound reason, L1.** The exclusion rule is the type group's published position four times over: the 2011 paper (`exclusion.tick:141-152`), the 2012 Types chapter (`types.tick:355-376`), Naden's "blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic benefits and the simplicity of the restriction" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:496-497`), POPL 2019's [Anc-Same-Trait]. Under the rule a nested tower whose every level carries the self-typed algebra traits at its own type is impossible: one `ZZ32` would be `Equality` at five instantiations. The WD's own types chapter says the numeric types "are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them" (`types-vals-vars.tex:502`), kept word for word in 2012. Steele's 2016 talk draws the tower flat. Route C, the patents' forest rule, was built as a shadow and priced (F-46): its soundness rule is the revival's, not the team's, and it needs code-generator, walk and checker work the team never did. The 2011 paper's own argument for the rule cites Java ("it is already required in Java") and decidability; that is the team's L1 word making an L3 argument, and it is theirs to make.
- **L2 confirms, does not decide.** The checker's Return Type Rule relies on the rule (F-44, measured by `IncompatibleClassChangeError`); the team's JVM type mapping relies on it (`TypeMapping.tex:125`, Chase 2012, not cited by the exclusion notes); the prelude was flattened in 2009-2010 with no stated reason. These say the compiled path needs the rule; they do not say the language has it. The language's texts say that.
- **Where the entry misstates.** Its "Why" is L2→L1 and misdated: "the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way" (2009 code, earlier than every text above; his phrase "the team's last record" was about the forest rule, rq 219), "and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper" (the paper keeps the rule and has no numbers and no tower; he was told on 09-24 that "the fact underneath it is narrower than you read it"). "He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen" joins the two meanings of specialisation and he said it was not an answer (rq 220). He was not shown the WD's "mutually exclusive" sentence when he chose (J0929 D4 found its absence from the brief), nor the right authors and dates (fixed 10-12). Both omissions understated the L1 case for the decision he took.
- **Default:** stands. The "Why" becomes the L1 grounds above, with the prelude's flat shape named as the team's compiled-world instance of the same answer and F-46 as the price of route C. The two sentences of rq 219 and 220 go to history. His (he held P-43 for his answer; one line to him).

### Tenet 6. The phase order (P-33). Holds, text.

- **Sound reason, L2 (a work plan).** The checker is the gate the compiled path runs first; code generation and the run time come after it; the natives are the switch-over's definition. The order was approved with phase 4 undesigned and its code-generation half unmeasured (W1 was launched after the yes). F-34 now measures that half at 52 walls.
- **Where the entry misstates.** "The interpreter's whole library" is wider than F-53's twelve, and his 10-26 goal says "the fuller library". No step names the bound flip (F-289). J1024 §6 already ruled the exit restated and two phase-4 zeros; I confirm. The 40 other components (F-290: 624 errors, 25 crashes) do not block the switch-over; they block P-12's step, so each reaches zero before that step or before the first program that needs it. That is the coordinator's view, his to confirm; it is sound.
- **Default:** phase 3 closes with 22c (ruling 5); P-33's phase 3 text restated as the thirteen under the compile command's own setting; phase 4 carries two zeros (the checker's and the code generator's over the thirteen); the 40 components placed before P-12's step. His (reads anew P-33's exit).

### Tenet 7. Unboxed doubles and `double[]` arrays (P-17, P-84). Holds, text.

- **Sound reason.** L1: the language's aim (`philosophy.tex`), value objects "an implementation may freely copy" (`objects.tex:38`), a `LinearSequence` of a value type "describes a sequence of 'unboxed' values" (`binary.tex:80`), Jan Maessen's note that the store under a sized array is what is unboxed (`future.tex:42`), the library's `nat` sizes on `Vector` and `Matrix`. L2: the code generator boxes every number (F-11); boxing is the main cost in Java models of microGPT's three kernels (row 306); the team's own direction is `Unbox.java` and the loader's empty "expando" stub. The entries cite the L2 measurement and the sizes; they do not cite `objects.tex:38` or `binary.tex:76-82`, which are the L1 grounds that answer "is unboxing the language's intent or only ours".
- **Where the record is inconsistent.** He was told on 09-19 that stamping "only renames", so no generic instance can hold a `double[]`; on 09-24 that "unboxing will build on" stamping. Both are L2 statements and both can be true (the class loader's way, A4, is unmeasured); the record must say so in one place. His 09-20 lean for the class-loader way was "recorded as your leans, to confirm" and is in no entry. Decision A (the mechanism under `double[]`) is the open risk of the "fast" half, as J0929 omission 3 said; nothing since measured it.
- **Default:** stands. Add the two L1 grounds; record his 09-20 lean under P-85 as a lean to confirm; state that stamping alone gives no `double[]` field and that A4 is unmeasured. Not consequential (text); the lean is his and goes to him as "to confirm".

### Tenet 8. The natives' form (P-58). Holds; his informed yes owed.

- **Sound reason, L3 with L1 practice.** The language has no foreign-function interface: the WD lists one among proposals (`future.tex:675`) and says nothing else. So the binding form is outside the language, an L3 choice, and the library's own practice decides it (P-27): every one of the 424 bindings is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The team built both forms, `builtinPrimitive` for walk and `import java` for the compiler, and chose neither for the library. The entry's ground "the specification prints `builtinPrimitive`'s declaration" is weak: it is true only through the included library api, whose comment describes walk's mechanism. The sound ground is the layer and the practice.
- **What J1024 already ruled** stands: the yes must be informed and must come before climb batch 23, since after 449 bindings move the other form costs a library sweep.
- **Default:** stands as decided; his informed yes before batch 23. Consequential; his. The rewrite states the layer and the window in which the choice is cheap to undo.

### Tenet 9. Walk runs the checker after the switch-over (P-12, P-59). Holds as a direction; its size is understated.

- **Sound reason.** L1: Fortress is statically typed (`philosophy.tex:14`); coercion is resolved statically (`conversions-coercions.tex`). L2: walk has no static types; the checker inserts `CoercionInvocation` nodes. P-59 accepts walk's run-time choice as the interpreter's limit until then; R0929 §1.11 strengthened that reading (walk cannot implement the team's last dispatch model either).
- **Where the entry misstates.** "A small change of its own" (the coordinator's 09-29 words, not his) is wrong by reading: walk runs with Scala off and "The Java version of the type checker is gone now" (`StaticChecker.java:228-229`); walk has no case for `CoercionInvocation` (grep over `interpreter/` finds none); walk would then take the checker's own departures (rows 470, 731) as its own; and F-290's 624 errors stand between the checker and the components walk's programs import. P-59's "microGPT's static types are concrete" is the coordinator's premise, unmeasured (rq 221), measurable only when microGPT compiles.
- **Default:** P-12 stands as the direction; its text names the three pieces (the Scala checker on for walk, walk reading the inserted nodes, the components cleared) and says the size is unmeasured. P-59 stands; its premise sentence marked as the coordinator's, to be measured. Not consequential (direction unchanged).

## 4. The bound: P-42 holds, on these grounds

**L1.** (a) POPL 2019, the type group's last published word, Steele and Ryu among the authors: "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any" (`ParkPOPL2019.txt:418-419`). (b) The WD's `Object` sentence (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`) is absent from the 2008 release (page 67), enters the repository in two bulk imports of 2009-11, the first in a chapter headed "Not Yet Implemented Features"; its composer is not recoverable. The same WD section says "Type parameters are instantiated with types such as trait types, tuple types, and arrow types" (`:53-54`), and the WD puts tuples, arrows and `()` outside `Object` (`types-vals-vars.tex:136`, `:215-216`); so under the WD's own `Object` default no unbounded parameter could take what the WD says parameters take. (c) The library, the team's statement of the language's library, declares its element parameters unbounded and instantiates them at tuples (`Generator[\E\]`, `zip`'s `(E,F)`); only six functions write `extends Any`. (d) The 2012 Types chapter states no default and makes `Any` the top with `Object` excluding `Void` and every tuple type (`types.tick:232-238`); Welterweight and the 2011 paper have `Any` as the top. (e) The team's own 2008 commit left the bound "(either Object or Any)" open. Naden's August 2012 theory calls `Object` "the distinguished top type" in a calculus with no tuples or arrows, where the two names coincide; it is not a vote for `Object` over tuples.

**L2, the archaeology's finding and how to read it.** Steele implemented the WD's sentence on 2012-05-28 ("amazingly, this was not yet implemented"), inserting `extends Any` into the compiled libraries and nine tests wherever they instantiated at `()`, a tuple, an arrow or `Any`; commented it out on 05-29 "so that interpreter tests will pass"; and on 05-30 made it a setting, on in `useCompilerLibraries`, off in `useInterpreterLibraries`. The brief's phrase "Steele's 2012 code chose `Object` as the language's rule" reads too much into it. His message says he was implementing a sentence already written, not deciding one; when the sentence broke walk's tests he did not change walk or the library, he confined the sentence to the compiled path; and he had to write `Any` by hand everywhere the compiled world needed tuples. No team text says the code generator, class loader or RTTI needs `Object` (archaeology §2.6, §5). The code reads the other way: Naden's dispatcher ignores a written `Any` bound as "meaningless" and checks any other (`OverloadSet.java:1516-1517`); `FnNameInfo.boundsFor` names an empty clause `Object` only in a generic method's name, which declaration and call compute alike. The team's texts after 2012-05-30 (Types, 05-31; Naden, 08-31; POPL 2019) do not carry `Object` as the default. So the setting is the compiled path's departure from the language's rule, L2, and ends by one line.

**L2, the probe.** Under `Any`, generic functions, objects, traits, dispatch to a generic arm and `typecase` at a pair or an arrow compile, load and run, making the same classes and the same bytecode as with `extends Any` written; the 23 `CompilerSystem` `.test` files pass under both settings; `ant testQuick` under `Any` gives 12 failures in 10 compiler tests, all test-side (one promotion, three pinned texts, four `where [\E extends Object\]` workarounds of row 412, one premise, one prelude limit). Under `Object`, `q = id((3, 4))` compiles and runs `id(3)`, printing `q + 1 = 4` (row 691 reached by row 412): the compile command as it stands can silently miscompile. `()` dies under either bound (row 339, confirmed by `javap`); a generic dotted method with a single tuple-typed parameter dies under either bound (new, `CodeGen.java:6250-6263`, the team's comment "when generics can be parametrized by tuples"). Neither depends on the bound.

**L3.** `java.lang.Object` is translated to Fortress `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:447`); natives are written against `fortress.AnyType.Any`; no team text ties Fortress `Object` to `java.lang.Object`. Java interoperability argues for `Any`, and the record never used an L3 ground for the bound. His hunch that layers were mixed is right in form; the crossing was L1→L2 on 09-20 (a WD sentence kept as the reason for a compiled-path setting), not L3→L1.

**What he was told, and whether it changes the decision.** Told: that the compile path writes `Object` and this refuses tuples (true); that Steele switched the bound off in 2012 for the interpreter tests (true, half the story); that the Types chapter has `Object` exclude function types (wrong: it puts arrows under `Object`); that "nothing in the code changes because of it" (wrong: `Shell.java:372`). Not told: that Steele turned it on for the compiled path as a setting on 05-30; the code that reads the bound; the sentence's absence from 1.0. Had he been told all of it, the question under P-26 would have been "is Steele's 2012 setting the team's later word on the language?", and the answer above is no. His yes rested on the tuples; the tuples decide it. The decision stands and is stronger.

**Where the entry misstates.** "Functions" (rq 218): the WD puts arrows outside `Object`, the Types chapter inside; drop the word, as the specification's callout already does. "The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure": the switch-over ends nothing by itself; `Shell.java:372` does, and no step named it (F-289, 685 errors under the command's setting).

**Defaults.** P-42 stands (his; no change). The flip lands in 22c as one small rung: `Shell.java:372` to `false`, `XXXImplicitBoundAny` promoted, three pinned diagnostics rewritten, four `comprises` tests written `where [\E\]`, `XXXOverrideGenericReturnTypeNotSubtype`'s premise rewritten with row 653 named, `CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC` given `T extends Object` with a comment naming the prelude's `||` until the switch-over (the smallest edit that keeps the test's purpose; the other way is an `XXX` test). The probe's record actions: a ledger row for the tuple-domain dotted-method defect (section 12 of the ledger); row 339's "unverified" dropped; row 691's note; F-289 updated at the landing; the two FACTS the probe hands over. The flip is the coordinator's to schedule (P-42 promised it), named to him because he listed it among 22c's candidates.

## 4. The library route and its premise (10-26, 04:31 to 05:25)

- Ask 2 (is phase 3 done, its exit restated) led to his statement of the goal (04:47:50): "The whole point of the switch-over is to avoid the need to port walk's library into the compiler's library. The revival is continuing the development of the type checker, so that it would accept the fuller Fortress library that the interpreter uses." P-37 lacks this reason; it goes in with the rewrites (section 8).
- The history, read in full at his insistence (`postmortem-2026-09-19/direction-history-transcripts.md`, `two-libraries.md`, `library-route-judgement.md`): on 09-15 he did not know there were two libraries; at 23:51 on 09-15 he asked "Couldn't the path forward be just to use the FortressLibrary for compiler as well?"; a probe (00:13 on 09-16) found 95% of the library plain Fortress, but desugaring and code generation were never reached; the coordinator put the fork twice as "not needed yet" (09-16) and on 09-17 chose the porting route for him, unpriced, and he accepted an order of steps; on 09-20 the post-mortem found this; his words "we need to unify this. into single library", "the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it" (P-37). Maessen's 2008 comment calls the switch a "hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly" (its reason Java imports, not the checker); the team left no plan to end the split and grew the prelude until June 2012; the specification knows one library.
- **The other 40 components** (624 errors, 25 crashes, F-290) are outside phase 3's twelve. He agreed the plan never meant them for phase 3 ("Of course"), but the goal is the fuller library. My view, his to confirm: they do not block the switch-over; they block P-12's step (walk runs the checker), so each reaches zero before that step or before the first program that needs it.

## 5. The foundations review (approved 06:11:21)

**Scope, nine tenets, each ground filed by the three layers:** 1 the goal (P-7, P-8); 2 the team's later word (P-26); 3 one library (P-37), premise that the compiled path can run it, not only check it; 4 the bound `Any` (P-42); 5 the exclusion rule and flat numbers (P-43); 6 the phase order (P-33); 7 unboxed doubles and `double[]` (P-17, P-84); 8 the natives' form (P-58); 9 walk runs the checker (P-12, P-59).

**Step 1, done.**
- `reviews/foundations/bound-archaeology.md` (`ab2ee0c29`): the Working Draft's `Object` sentence is not in 1.0 (2008), first in bulk imports of 2009-11; later team texts split (Welterweight, the 2011 paper, POPL 2019 p. 11:9 give `Any`; Naden 2012 calls `Object` "the distinguished top type"; a 2008 commit left "either Object or Any" open). Steele wrote the compiled path's `Object` default on 2012-05-28 (`91e71e62e`, "amazingly, this was not yet implemented", writing `extends Any` into the compiled libraries and tests that take tuples, arrows or `()`), turned it off on 05-29 "so that interpreter tests will pass" (`c61723f61`), and made it a setting, on for the compiled path, on 05-30 (`afb02f41d`). On 09-29 he was told the compiled path writes `Object` and that Steele switched it off for the interpreter tests, but not that Steele switched it on for the compiled path as the language's rule; two statements of mine that day were wrong (the sentence's date; "the Types chapter has `Object` exclude function types").

## 7. The flat numbers: my framing corrected (07:46:17)

I had framed the judge's question as whether the prelude's flat numbers are a design of the language or a JVM measure. He corrected me: the record's digging decided the flat tower, and I was wrong. The grounds on record: the exclusion rule in the team's language texts (the 2011 paper, `exclusion.tick:141-152`; the 2012 Types chapter, `types.tick:355-376`; Naden 2012, "blanket … for the semantic benefits and the simplicity"; POPL 2019 keeps it); under the rule a nested tower is impossible (`ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, both `Integral` at different arguments); the Working Draft says the number types "are mutually exclusive" (`types-vals-vars.tex:502`); Steele's 2016 talk shows a flat tower; the checker relies on the rule (F-44) and so does the JVM mapping (`TypeMapping.tex:125`); routes A, B and C weighed 09-22 to 09-24 (`reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md`, `reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md`, `reviews/mie-probes/`), A chosen 09-24; reviews D4 (09-29), the POPL recheck and V5 (10-23) keep it. What is open is narrower: P-43's stated reason, "the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way", is the weakest ground and not his words (rq 219). The judge's real question for P-37: when does a design of the compiler's prelude bind the one library? 12:- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).
16:- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
25:- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.
34:- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library. The decision is not put to him again. How the checker comes to accept the library, its first step and the order of the work, was left to a plan for him, which he approved (P-33).
67:- P-156 **A collection's index type extends `Index`, a trait that the ranges exclude, and a tuple of indices is an `Index`.** Every index parameter of the library's generic indexed types is bounded `I extends Index`; `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes it. So a subscript that takes one index and a subscript that takes a range never apply to the same value, and the pair is a valid overloading at every instance. A tuple type whose elements are all `Index` types is itself an `Index`, on both paths and in the specification: a typing rule that changes no value, so `m[i, j]` passes its tuple `(i, j)` as before. Why: it is the team's own fix for this pair (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`), its "magic" read as subtyping. A `where` constraint `I excludes Range[\I\]` was weighed and not taken: the team left such a constraint as an open question, and the code generator refuses a `where` clause in a declaration's header. `Index` stands beside `Any` and `Object`, outside `Object`: it is declared `trait Index extends Any`, which the desugaring and walk keep as written and the traits chapter names as an exception to the rule that every trait extends `Object`, so a tuple of indices is an `Index` and never an `Object`, and P-42's tuples stay out of `Object`, as the specification's `trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }` keeps them. `BoundedRange`, which cannot take the bound, since the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56), keeps its narrowed `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` under the method condition `where { I extends Index }`, the library's form for a member that applies at some instances only; after the switch-over the code generator's refusal of a method with a `where` clause stops it too, as it stops `SumReduction`'s two `distribute`s (row 701). Row 783: the subscript pair.
68:- P-157 **`Vector` and `Matrix` stay additive groups, and the overloading check's exclusion test reads the self type and the static parameters' bounds, so the arrays' scalar `+` and `-` stand beside the vectors' own.** The team's `Vector` and `Matrix` extend `AdditiveGroup`, and the library's generic block of `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar (P-88) stays beside them. With symbolic operators checked (P-155), the checker refused 8 such pairs, though no call fits both: a vector's own `+` takes two vectors, the block's `+` an array and a number, and arrays exclude numbers. So the exclusion test reads a self-typed trait's `self` as `C[\X\] & X`, the fact that P-146's extender rule guarantees, and its existential reduction reads the static parameters' bounds (P-152); specificity and the Return Type Rule keep the plain signatures. Why: it keeps both the team's library as written and the revival's block, and it was his first stance; taking vectors out of `AdditiveGroup` would have bent the team's design for a gap of the checker. Reading bounds is the POPL 2019 paper's own reduction. Probe A1 measured it (`perf-probes/self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md`): the 8 gone, nothing else moved.
93:- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: whether the array factory chooses a store for each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets the `double[]` store (P-84), B is where unboxed arithmetic happens, and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.
94:- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** The model is microGPT's two programs; the vocabulary is the array operations that they are written in (`FlatArrays.fss` for C4, the flat program, and `FlatArrays2.fss` for the APL-style one). No operator in the model is replaced by a function call to pass an overload check, as a proposed repair once wrote `planeSum(mask, x)` for `mask + x`; the vocabulary changes instead. Any repair that changes a line of the model is shown to the curator as a diff before it is built. Decision D, still open and returning after the switch-over with the other array decisions (P-85), is such a diff: it gives C4's arrays sized types, in its vocabulary's signatures and in the model lines that these force (`explorations/reviews/decision-d-diff.md`; the patch itself is only in git, in the parent of `84aef6a4f`). Nothing of decision D is applied before microGPT compiles, after the switch-over.
13:- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. The specification states the same intent: its chapter on objects lets an implementation freely copy value objects, among them floating-point numbers, and its chapter on memory sequences makes a `LinearSequence` of a value type a sequence of "unboxed" values. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

content.content:
## 3. Question 2, decision A: what puts `double[]` under the library's generic array traits

**The question.** His decision of 2026-09-19 makes the store a JVM `double[]`, and the library's arrays are generic in their element type: `Vector[\T, nat s0\]` keeps its elements in `mem: PrimitiveArray[\T,s0\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2339-2345`). What makes a `Vector[\RR64, 16\]` hold a `double[]` while a `Vector[\T, 16\]` of another `T` keeps a boxed store?

**The mathematics.** None: the choice changes how the numbers are held, not what they mean.

**What each path does today.**

- Walk: every store is `PrimitiveArray`, boxed values in an `AtomicArray` (`coordinator/array-design.md` § 1). The team wrote one unboxed store: `object PrimImmutableRR64Array[\nat s0\]() extends ImmutableArray1[\RR64,0,s0\]` over a Java `double[]` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss:43-52`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/PrimImmutableRR64Array.java`). Jan Maessen, 2008-07-28: "Immutable arrays of unboxed RR64. When you request an immutable array of RR64 these should be used in preference to the boxed version" (`353818213`). No library file names it; nothing selects it.
- The compiled path: stamping renames classes and cannot produce a `double[]` field (`coordinator/array-design.md` § 2, probe 1). The only unboxed stores are two hand-written Java classes, `FZZ32Vector` over an `int[]` and `FStringVector`, lowered straight to their classes by a table in the code generator; every element read is boxed through seven frames; a native helper cannot take a Java array (FACTS § The territory map, line 160).
- What an unboxed store buys alone, measured on 2026-09-20: nothing. The dot product over a `double[]` read and written through a boxing accessor is 8.9 times primitive, against 6.4 times for boxed storage; the matrix product 6.6 against 6.2 (`reviews/array-design-review.md`, Serious 4; `compiler-probes/array-design-review/java-medians.tsv`). The traffic is unboxed only by decision B, phase 6 (PLAN.md).
- The library's selection device, measured here on both paths (`reviews/array-design-ways/probes/`, one private cache per path; the compiled path in the compiler's own world, since the switch-over has not happened):
  - `WayANoCast.fss`: a generic factory with the library's witness `typecase` (`array1`'s, `FortressLibrary.fss:2375-2379`) whose `RR64` arm returns a store written for `RR64` alone. The checker refuses it, "Function body has type OR(DStore,BStore[\T\]), but declared return type is Arr[\T\]", as on 2026-09-20; walk runs it and picks `DStore` for `RR64`.
  - `WayACast.fss`: the same arm through the library's `cast`, `cast[\Arr[\T\]\](DStore(...))`, the device of `additiveIdentity` (`FortressLibrary.fss:3140-3155`). The checker accepts it. The compiled run and walk both print `RR64 DStore 1.5` and `ZZ32 BStore 7`.
  - `WayACastSized.fss`: the same with sizes, `vec[\T, nat n\]` returning `cast[\Vec[\T,n\]\](DVec[\n\](...))`. Accepted; both paths pick `DVec[\16\]` for `RR64` and the generic store for `ZZ32`, and a function with a shared size takes two of them.
  - `WayASpec.fss`: specialisation by overloading, a plain `mk(w: () -> RR64, x: RR64)` beside the generic `mk[\T\](w: () -> T, x: T)`, called from generic code with the library's witness. The checker accepts it and the compiled run dispatches to the plain declaration for `RR64` and to the generic one for `ZZ32`. Walk refuses the pair when it loads the program, "has a parameter with generic type, at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types", its declaration-time family check (rows 159 and 475).

**The specification.**

- "Fortress arrays are complex data structures; simple linear storage is encapsulated by the HeapSequence type, which is used in the implementation of arrays" (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`), marked not yet supported (`:15-16`).
- Jan Maessen's note on unboxed types, recorded in the draft: "Do we want to permit arrays of fixed bounds to be unboxed? No. Unboxed arrays are a different other thing. Among other things, an array of fixed bounds may be a segment of another array" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:42`). The sized array is a structure; the linear store under it is what is unboxed.
- Jan's own example of the selection, in the draft's future work on overloading by static parameters: `array1[\T extends Object, nat s0\]()` beside `array1[\T extends Number, nat s0\](): Vector[\T,s0\]` (`future.tex:236-246`). The library's `array1` does it with the witness `typecase` meanwhile, "TODO: fix when Number is covariant" (`FortressLibrary.fss:2374`).
- The compiled encoding: "mentions of static parameters are replaced with their upper bounds" (`Papers/Implementation/MethodMapping.tex:134`), which is why stamping renames and nothing more.

**The commits.** David Chase's unboxing plan, "Cases for unboxing: 1) primitive. ZZ{8,16,32,64}, RR{32,64}, Boolean ... 3) unboxed fields" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:21-27`, first in `bce8b45ae`, 2009-03-07), referenced by nothing; and the loader's place for it, "if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff." (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`, first in `4179cee84`, 2009-07-29).

**The peers.**

- .NET: "When a generic type is first constructed with a value type as a parameter, the runtime creates a specialized generic type ... Specialized generic types are created one time for each unique value type"; for reference types one shared version (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/generics-in-the-run-time). A loader-made class per instantiation.
- Java: "JEP 218: Generics over Primitive Types", status Candidate: "extend generic types to support the specialization of generic classes and interfaces over primitive types" (https://openjdk.org/jeps/218).
- Scala: `@specialized` makes the compiler "generate specialized versions of generic code for specified types" (https://www.scala-lang.org/api/2.13.x/scala/specialized.html); Spire warns that "specialization will increase bytecode size by a factor of x2-10" (https://spire-math.org/guide.html).
- Haskell: `Data.Vector.Unboxed` "picks an efficient, specialised representation for every element type" through a data family chosen by the `Unbox` class (https://hackage-content.haskell.org/package/vector-0.13.2.0/docs/Data-Vector-Unboxed.html). A representation per element type, selected by the type.
- Julia, C++ and Rust compile a copy per concrete type (`reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md` § 6).

**The ways.** Every way but A4 needs a hand-written Java store over `double[]`, on the `FZZ32Vector` pattern, and a Fortress object for it written for `RR64` alone, as `PrimImmutableRR64Array` is; they differ in what selects it.

1. **A1, the library's selection device with the library's `cast`** (`WayACast`, `WayACastSized`, measured). The generic factories `vector`, `matrix`, `array1` to `array3` and their tabulated forms test the witness and return the `RR64` store through `cast` for `RR64`, the generic store otherwise. The library's text keeps its generic types; the model's `vector[\RR64,s\]` gets the unboxed store with no line of its own. The cast is one run-time type test per array made, not per element (my reading). The draft's own spelling of the same selection is overloading by the element type's bound (`future.tex:236-246`); it still needs the cast to return a store written for one type (my reading).
2. **A2, specialisation by overloading on the witness** (`WayASpec`, measured). A plain factory for `RR64` beside the generic one; dispatch chooses from generic code. No cast. 12-: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.
13-
14:## What an entry is
15-
16-An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17-
18-- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19-- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
20-- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
21-- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
22-- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
23-- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
24-- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
25-- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
26-- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
27-- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
28-- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
29-- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
30-- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.
31-
32-Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
33-
34-1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
35-2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
36-3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
37-4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
38-5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
39-6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.
--
100-
101-- The mining workflow finds where each POSITIONS entry came from: the curator's words, or an agent's summary or default. Run it on the entries that it has not traced, before the clarity workflow rewrites them. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/README.md`.
102:- The clarity workflow rewrites POSITIONS or FACTS entries so that each reads on its own. For FACTS, it first judges every entry by the six checks of "What an entry is" (scope, present meaning, evidence, comprehension, ownership and consistency), and rewrites only those marked reword or reorganize. Run it when entries no longer read on their own. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md`.
103-- The orientation workflow writes `fortress-repo`'s revival part, the short account of how revived Fortress differs from the original, which every worker reads whole. Its consolidate mode rewrites the whole part. Run it when a cold read or the regression quiz shows that the part no longer reads whole, or when an update cannot keep it within the README's budget. Its update mode runs after each landing (`references/batch.md`, "The landing"). Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/README.md`.
104-
105-## INDEX and the gap ledger
106-
107-- Give each new note under `explorations/` one line in INDEX, from its header comment's first sentence.
108-- Put a run's working files in an `evidence/` folder beside its results file: its briefs, chunks and checks, and the worker reports that the results draw on. Move them there with `git mv` once the results are judged. Only the results file gets an INDEX line. `check-index.sh` skips evidence folders. Do not add a folder's name to its list to let the folder pass.
109-- The gap ledger keeps its rows in topic sections. A row keeps its number for good. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` is the only way to write it. Other views, such as `explorations/apl/lessons.md`, are derived from it.
110-- Split a rewrite of the ledger among small workers, each with a slice of rows that it can hold. Run a duplicate search first, as its own step.
111-- Ask the curator before you regroup the ledger's rows or derive its views again.

3:- P-27 **Whoever extends the library follows the library's own practice.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side. This rule governs how the library is extended. It does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language, such as the self type as the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude write it: the team's later word, dated against the texts, decides between them (P-26).
4-  by: the clarity pass; note: title narrowed to the body and its limit stated, from the foundations trap test (explorations/reviews/foundations/evidence/trap-test/grades.md section 4, POSITIONS 27, scenario 2: "the dated later word does"); limited to designs of the language, since the foundations judgement tenet 8 uses P-27 for the natives' binding form, outside the language; old title "The library's own practice is the standard."
5-- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the team's later texts point, if weakly, toward the rule, and peer languages share it. The compiler's prelude writes the self type as a `comprises T` clause instead, and that form does not bind the library: Naden's write-up on the Return Type Rule (P-26 names it), later than the team's last edits of that clause, puts the self type in bounds only, the form `X extends C[\X\]` that the library writes. F-225 states the rule as built and holds the dates.
